1 ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
2
3 Analysis of this case begins with the burden of proof. The
4 Assessor' s original value is presumed to be correct and can only be
5 overcome by presentation of clear, cogent, and convincing evidence
6 that the Assessor' s value is erroneous. 13 Clear, cogent, and
7 convincing" evidence means a quantum of proof which is less than
8 beyond a reasonable doubt, but more than a mere preponderance of the
9 evidence. It is the quantum of evidence necessary to convince the
10 trier of fact that the ultimate issue is " highly probable". 14
11
12 Chapter 84. 41 RCW, Revaluation of Property, governs the proce-
13 dures and methods whereby the value of property is determined
14 including physical inspections, valuations, and adjustments based on
15 statistical data under a plan filed with and approved by the Depart-
16 ment of Revenue.
17
18 Chapter 84. 40 RCW, Listing of Property, establishes statutory
19 requirements that all property is valued as of the first day of
20 January of the year in which assessed at 100 percent of true and fair
21 value and sets the criterion of valuation.
22

24 produces non- uniform results and, therefore, does not produce true and

9 During the Owner' s argument, he stated on several occasions that
10 all one needed was to " do the algebra" or " do the mathematics" using
11 his equation and the answer to valuation would be readily apparent.
12 The answer to valuation is not so easily reached. We conclude with
13 the following trenchant observation on the reality of property valua-
14 tion:
15 Absent a miracle of time, place and circumstances --
willing buyer, willing seller, high noon, January 1, 1984,
16 for example -- true market value for purposes of ad valorem
taxation is always an estimate, always an expression of
17 judgment, always a result built on a foundation of supposi-
tions about knowledgeable and willing buyers and sellers
18 endowed with money and desire, whose desires are said to
converge in a dollar description of the asset. All of this
19 is simply a sophisticated effort at " let' s pretend" or
modeling", in modern jargon, and all of it involves judg-
20 ment. Not natural law, not science—judgment.
21 Emphasis added.) Union Pacific R. R. Co. v. State Tax Comm' n of Utah,
22 716 F. Supp. 543, 544 ( D. Utah, 1988), Jenkins, Chief Judge.
23
24 This Board concludes the Owner has not met the clear, cogent, and
25 convincing standard necessary to overcome the presumption in favor of
26 the Assessor' s valuation.
